data.title: Gilead kicks off Latino AIDS Awareness Day with new campaign
data.description:
With Oct. 15 marking National Latino AIDS Awareness Day, the time is “Ahorita Mismo" (Right Now!) to push for HIV prevention education in Hispanic and Latino communities, as Gilead Sciences expresses in its new campaign. 

The latest offshoot of Gilead's Care for the Culture initiative, the company's Ahora Mismo campaign targets Latino communities through trusted voices and culturally significant humor, a lane that's emerging as one right up Gilead’s alley. 

“While significant progress has been made in HIV prevention, gaps in awareness, stigma and access to information continue to impact many communities — including and especially Latino communities,” Gilead’s VP of marketing and U.S. prevention Ashley Gildea commented in an emailed statement. “Ahorita Mismo - meaning ‘right now’ - is a call to action rooted in the belief that timely information can help people make informed decisions about their health.”

"Through culturally grounded storytelling and community-centered engagement, this campaign seeks to elevate awareness of HIV testing and prevention options, spark meaningful conversations, and help ensure the Latino community has the information and support they need to take the next step toward protecting their health," Gildea said. 

The company’s minute-long “Ahorita Ghosted” spot, one of three that goes with the campaign, stars popular digital creators Eric Sedeño and Boman Martinez-Reid, the latter of whom will soon be seen in a Scottish castle in an upcoming season of Peacock’s hit reality show “The Traitors.” 

In the video, a retro display with a funky font and a catchy, Latin music-inspired background tune welcomes viewers to “1-800-Ahorita,” where “dating advance and HIV prevention get real” through fictional calls that speak to real-life situations. Sedeño and Martinez-Reid sit across each other in a comfy, realistic living room set under a neon “1-800-Ahorita” sign. After an unsuccessful round of rock paper scissors, the phone rings with their first caller, who shares the story of a man who “straight up ghosted” him. 

The potential reason for the ghost is soon revealed, and it’s not “accidentally liking one of his posts from 2019,” as Sedeño initially suggests. The man on the phone expresses that all he did was ask if his partner had been tested for HIV, a situation that Martinez-Reid maintains is “still salvageable.” Sedeño asks if the caller himself has been tested, which he was planning to “ahorita” (right now).

“Don’t ghost your sexual health,” Sedeño says in the video. “The impact of HIV continues to affect the Latino community.”

“A conversation with your healthcare provider about getting tested and learning your HIV prevention options can go a long way,” Martinez-Reid adds, to which Sedeño agrees. 

“Our health is something we should take care of ahorita mismo,” he says. The duo has successfully reassured the caller, leaving the two to end the ad with a jokey exchange and a silly montage of the friends posing in the living room set as a voiceover directs viewers to Gilead's Care for the Culture website. 

Related

Otters, bears and Pharma Lions: inside Gilead’s bronze-winning Cannes spot

Throughout the video, Sedeño and Martinez-Reid seamlessly slip in references familiar to the Latino community such as Sedeño calling the caller “corazón,” a common Spanish term of endearment. The digital creators repeat a similiar song and dance in "Ahorita Eggplant" and "Ahorita Throuple," in which they encourage other callers who reach out with sticky dating situations to meet with a healthcare provider to discuss their HIV status. 

Black and Hispanic communities both experience a greater HIV burden, according to Gilead and Emory University’s AIDSVu. In 2024, Hispanic/Latino individuals represented 34% of all new HIV diagnoses in the U.S., despite making up only 19% of the population, and had an HIV prevalence rate that was more than three times higher than for white individuals. 

Care for the Culture looks to emphasize the importance of HIV prevention across these communities, reminding its audience that “HIV is not somewhere else. It’s right here,” the website says, noting that seven out of every ten estimated new HIV infections occurred within Black and Latino communities as of 2022.

In Care for the Culture’s efforts to strike up conversations around HIV and destigmatize testing and prevention, Gilead previously used the power of music and renowned R&B singer TLC’s Tionne “T-Boz” Watkins in “So We PrEP,” a remix of TLC’s 1994 hit “Creep.”  

More recently, Gilead has looked to reach Black communities through other Care for the Culture initiatives such as its “Up to Date” campaign, which saw comedian and podcast host Nicole Byers using culturally relevant language and humor to spread HIV education in a spot that also included “Saturday Night Live” alum Devon Walker. 

Both “Up to Date” and “Ahorita” include storylines and verbiage that are relatable to modern dating and sexual culture, such as the late-night hook-up depicted in “Up to Date” or the ghosting conundrum in “Ahorita.” The topical tropes speak to Gilead’s evolving messaging around HIV as the company moves beyond scientific-focused content to centering “authenticity” and directness, executive director of public affairs, U.S. advocacy and health equity Deborah Wafer explained in a July interview with Fierce. 

“We need to be more direct and talk about sex and talk about prevention of HIV,” Wafer said, with one way to do so being through “the right language” that younger generations can pick up on. 

As the maker of the first-ever pre-exposure prophylaxis (PrEP) option back in 2012, Gilead has been at the forefront of HIV prevention and, in turn, HIV drug marketing since the beginning. The company’s collection of HIV products includes top-selling treatment Biktarvy, daily PrEP Descovy and most recently long-acting PrEP injection Yeztugo. In 2025, Gilead picked up $20.8 billion in HIV-specific sales, a 6% jump from 2024.

data.title: Compass puts resistant depression on the map with awareness day
data.description:
Compass Pathways has partnered with mental health organizations on the first-ever awareness day for treatment-resistant depression (TRD). 

The biotech, which is developing a drug candidate based on the active ingredient in magic mushrooms, is working on the awareness day with the National Alliance on Mental Illness, Mental Health America and the Depression and Bipolar Support Alliance (DBSA). The mental health organizations are sharing information and resources about TRD. 

Compass quoted data showing that TRD affects an estimated 4 million people in the U.S., of whom fewer than 5% are on a treatment indicated for the form of depression. Johnson & Johnson’s Spravato became the first monotherapy approved for adults with TRD in the U.S. in January 2025. 

J&J has worked to raise awareness of depression, including by launching its “Generation Fine” campaign in May. However, physicians continue to see gaps in awareness of TRD, as Sagar Parikh, M.D., vice chair of DBSA’s scientific advisory board, explained in a statement. 

“When depression continues despite multiple treatment attempts, many people do not realize they may be experiencing TRD,” Parikh said. “TRD Awareness Day can help both patients and clinicians better understand that this is a distinct condition, separate from major depressive disorder, and recognize when it may be time to ask different questions about care strategies.”

Aiming to launch its TRD drug in the first half of 2027, Compass is preparing for commercialization. Last month, the biotech launched “Change the Tune in TRD,” an education campaign focused on U.S. healthcare providers. Compass is running the campaign to provide evidence-based education on the longer, more persistent episodes associated with TRD. 

Alongside the awareness day unveiling, the company shared details of its efforts to understand the lives of people with TRD. A Compass survey found nearly 95% of TRD patients describe themselves as either functioning but struggling, surviving day to day or barely getting by. 

The impacts extend beyond patients with TRD. Almost two in three caregivers say TRD impacts the whole family’s social, physical or mental health. More than half of people say that caregiving has taken a major toll on their mental health. Compass plans to share the full survey report in the future.

data.title: Sanofi dodges fine over alleged disparagement of CSL flu vaccine
data.description:
Sanofi has avoided a European Union fine after antitrust regulators accepted its commitments to address the alleged disparagement of CSL Seqirus’ rival flu vaccine.

The European Commission opened an antitrust investigation in June to assess whether Sanofi’s alleged disparagement campaign against CSL’s Fluad violated EU competition rules. Sanofi proposed pledges to resolve the case, leading the Commission to assess the impact of the company’s commitments in July and August. 

The Commission accepted Sanofi’s commitments Wednesday, sparing the company from antitrust fines it can impose for disparaging rivals. Teresa Ribera, the EU’s executive vice president for clean, just and competitive transition, explained the decision at a press conference.

Sanofi immediately approached the Commission “in a cooperative mood,” Ribera said. The company’s engagement enabled the Commission to quickly identify the remedies to ensure “a prompt reaction and a prompt enforcement of the law,” she said, adding that the resolution was “good, sufficient and immediate,” the official added. 

Ribera pushed back on a reporter’s suggestion that sparing Sanofi from a fine would encourage other companies to disparage their rivals. The speed with which Sanofi reacted to the investigation showed that “they are absolutely convinced of our capacity to be tough on this,” she said. Ribera expects Sanofi to comply with the commitments, but her team “will remain vigilant on what they are doing.”

Legally binding commitments prohibit Sanofi from making certain statements in promotional materials aimed at healthcare professionals in Germany and France. Until March 2030, Sanofi cannot criticize, cast doubt upon or contradict national vaccination recommendations or highlight Fluad negatively, or unduly suggest that its own vaccine, Efluelda, is safer or more effective. 

For two years, Sanofi’s German and French websites must acknowledge that the applicable national vaccination recommendations treat Fluad and Efluelda as equivalent in protecting elderly people against the flu, both having a robust evidence base. Sanofi must send the statement to healthcare professionals and key opinion leaders in Germany who previously received the allegedly disparaging materials.

data.title: AbbVie slots in ‘Time For Treks’ with CLL community walk
data.description:
AbbVie, the National Park Foundation (NPF) and CLL Society are working together to immerse people with chronic lymphocytic leukemia (CLL) in the beauty of community and the great outdoors with a new “Time For Treks” campaign. 

Kicking off Oct. 17, the organizations will host a free blood cancer community walk at Cabrillo National Monument in San Diego, California. The event is welcome to people with CLL, caregivers and supporters and focuses on fostering outdoor experiences and connections within the community. 

“Because every person's experience with CLL is different, every trek can look different, too,” CLL Society reminded potential trekkers on its LinkedIn page, encouraging visitors to “choose the route and pace that feels right for you.” 

The campaign stems from AbbVie’s deep understanding of the CLL patient community, “not just as patients, but as people,” senior director of patient advocacy, oncology portfolio Christine Armstrong explained in an interview with Fierce. According to Armstrong, one activity that has come up “time and time again” in discussions with patients is a love of the outdoors and hiking with friends and family. 

“Time For Treks” naturally came to life when the company pondered how it can continue to “really meet patients where they are,” Armstrong said. The initiative’s name signifies the moments during a patient’s treatment journey where they get a chance to step away and perhaps engage in a nature-based activity. 

“The campaign itself, it was really co-created with patients,” Armstrong said. 

One patient whose insights helped form the program is Alejandro, an environmental engineer with CLL who was featured in AbbVie’s 2025 short film “Second Winds.” The documentary saw CLL patients Alejandro, Christina and Jeff sharing their individual stories and staying active through activities such as hiking, biking and more. Alejandro’s input was “reminiscent of many other patients’ insights about loving to be outdoors,” Armstrong noted. 

Related

AbbVie short film showcases 'Second Winds' of life after CLL diagnosis

AbbVie and the National Park Foundation have plans to expand the initiative to other national parks in the future, as both align on a mission to “encourage people to get out” and plan treks within their own communities or local parks. 

Between the joint priorities of the National Park Foundation, AbbVie, the CLL society and the patient community, “I think that this is that kind of perfect synergized campaign,” Armstrong said. 

At the launch on Oct. 17, AbbVie will leverage its educational website on navigating and managing CLL, which contains information on treatment options and approaches as well as other tips and resources for living with CLL. 

AbbVie has been supporting CLL patients through its Johnson & Johnson-partnered BTK inhibitor Imbruvica since its initial 2013 approval and its Genentech-partnered BCL-2 inhibitor Venclexta, which first hit the market in 2016. 

In 2024, the company dug into the emotional experience of a CLL diagnoses with a survey that was the first to break down the results by race/ethnicity to highlight the differing mental health impacts and desired support resources.

data.title: UCB fashions ‘Wear It Out’ project with empowering t-shirts
data.description:
UCB is encouraging people with immunology-driven diseases such as hidradenitis suppurativa (HS), plaque psoriasis and psoriatic arthritis (PsA) to wear their heart on their sleeve in a new community-driven program.  

For those living with chronic skin conditions such as psoriasis, HS and PsA, deciding what to wear each day can be a battle that goes beyond style. Those with plaque psoriasis may avoid black clothing due to fear of visible skin flaking on the fabric, while people with HS might worry about drainage or leaking from a disease flare showing up on white clothing. 

Patients with stiff or painful joints from PsA, meanwhile, may struggle with the act of getting dressed itself, especially when dealing with things such as buttons on clothes, UCB explained in a release. 

Now, the disease community can reclaim white and black t-shirts with “Wear It Out,” hallmarked by a one-of-a-kind, “condition-conscious” t-shirt line made by graphic artist Sophia Yeshi. Yeshi worked with patients and advocates to create designs that “reflects the beauty, courage and individuality of the community,” Yeshi noted. 

“My work explores themes of identity, resilience, and belonging, so when I was given the opportunity to create something beautiful out of the often challenging experiences of real people living with these conditions, I was so inspired,” Yeshi said in the release. "Every person who shared their story brought a unique perspective and sense of strength to this project.”

Printed on a custom blend of bamboo and organic cotton specifically meant to be a skin-safe, non-irritating blend for patients with the skin diseases, the t-shirts come in white and black and depict a colorful display of self-expression, featuring abstract people surrounded by a wave of blue, orange and purple hues. On the black and white t-shirts, the designs become “symbols of the choices others may never understand,” UCB said. 

Related

UCB partners with Dr. Pimple Popper in ongoing hidradenitis suppurativa campaign

“Getting dressed should not be a strategic decision, and feeling comfortable in your own body should never feel out of reach, but for many people with HS, PSO, or PsA, it can be [by] quietly ruling out a white or black shirt or skipping an invitation because of what the condition may show,” UCB’s head of patient strategy, U.S. immunology Brittany Blair explained. 

“Wear It Out transforms that quiet calculation into a visual community symbol worth celebrating and it is a reminder that no one should have to settle for less than feeling like themselves in their healthcare journey.”

“Wear It Out” shines a light on the unseen disease impacts of the approximately 2.5 million people living with HS in the U.S. and the some 11.3 million with psoriasis or PsA.  To get in on the wearable t-shirt aspect of the project, patients are encouraged to visit the associated campaign website to join the “Wear It Out” community, engage with educational and treatment resources and share their own story via audio or video to receive their own shirt. 

Patients must share their story to receive a shirt, but contributions don’t have to be lengthy and won’t be used by UCB without consent, the company emphasizes on the website. 

“Whether it’s just a thought or a more detailed experience, every story helps bring the Wear It Out program to life,” the website explains.

An “explore treatment” tab on the site directs patients to UCB’s product website for Bimzelx, the company’s FDA-approved biologic for psoriasis, PsA, non-radiographic axial spondyloarthritis, ankylosing spondylitis and HS. 

Last month, Bimzelx took the top spot on iSpot.TV’s monthly ranking of drug ad spending, reflecting both streaming data and traditional linear TV. According to iSpot, UCB spent a total of $56.9 million on Bimzelx streaming and linear ads in September as the company looks to further expand the reach of its immunology blockbuster.

data.title: Galderma sculpts new narrative around menopausal skin changes
data.description:
One in two women is unaware that hormonal fluctuations during perimenopause and menopause can affect their skin, a Galderma survey found.

Galderma, a dermatology specialist, recently worked with Perspectus Global to survey 5,090 women who have experienced or are experiencing perimenopause or menopause in the U.K., the U.S., Brazil and China. More than half of the respondents initially attributed menopause-related skin changes to general aging. Fewer than one-third of the women recognized the link to menopause.

The misconceptions affected skin care purchases, with 70% buying products designed to address signs of aging in response to skin changes during perimenopause or menopause. Almost half of the respondents struggled to find information, in part because advice focuses on aging over menopause. 

Galderma is working to fill the perceived advice gap ahead of World Menopause Day on Oct. 18. Framing its research as evidence of “The Menopausal Skin Misread,” the company has launched a campaign to share scientific evidence and women’s stories. The “Rewriting the Future of Your Skin, Own your Menopause Story” campaign includes a website that explains how hormonal changes affect the skin.

The survey points to demand for such information. More than 80% of respondents agreed that they would feel more informed and in control of their skin care decisions if they better understood the differences between general aging and menopause-related skin changes.

Galderma is launching the awareness drive following research into the effects of its Restylane Skinboosters and Sculptra products on menopausal women. The study, which Galderma supported, linked the use of Restylane Skinboosters followed by Sculptra to increased facial dermal thickness.

Sculptra, an injectable cosmetic, is a key product for Galderma. Double-digit Sculptra growth in the U.S. and international markets helped (PDF) Galderma’s filler and biostimulator sales rise 10.5% to $611 million in the second quarter. Galderma named geographic expansion of Sculptra sales as one of its five key opportunities for the rest of the year.

data.title: Invenra joins the ADC game with custom card deck
data.description:
Invenra has created playing cards featuring artwork by people affected by cancer as it seeks biopharma buy-in for its antibody-drug conjugate (ADC) service. 

The Wisconsin-based antibody service provider has started using its bispecific and trispecific antibody platforms to generate ADC targeting moieties. To support the rollout, Invenra has arrived at the World ADC Conference in San Diego with its “52 Views of Cancer” playing card deck. Each of the 52 cards, plus the jokers and box cover, features art that Invenra has licensed from people affected by cancer. 

Invenra CEO Roland Green came up with the idea for the deck while looking at artwork by his daughter, who was recently diagnosed with ovarian cancer. Viewing the artwork, Green envisioned “a collection of art that highlights the patients’ stories, with a goal of inspiring the scientists and clinicians in their effort to find cures,” the CEO said in a statement.

The “52 Views of Cancer” website displays each artwork and statements from the artists. The deck has a wide array of art styles, with the aces alone featuring a digital collage, an oil painting and a watercolor and ink piece. Their stories are similarly varied, reflecting the impact cancer has on patients and their loved ones.

Invenra’s deployment of the cards at the World ADC Conference is the start of an ongoing effort. The company plans to share the decks at other conferences to expose researchers, clinicians and scientists to patients’ voices and perspectives.

The deck adds to the long history of using playing cards for awareness and marketing. Bayer created a deck in the 1960s. Roche followed suit around 1980. More recently, Amylyx Pharmaceuticals used a playing card design to make its disease education website simpler and more approachable. And Maat Pharma created a version of the game “happy families” to educate people about the gut microbiota.

data.title: UCB’s Bimzelx takes the drug ad spending top spot
data.description:
UCB’s immunology drug Bimzelx has once again become the highest ranked drug in iSpot.TV’s pharma ad spending league as it topped the charts for September. 

The Belgian pharma’s med took no. 1 position as iSpot.TV has, as of September, started adding streaming data—as well as traditional linear TV—to its monthly analysis. 

This is because streaming is increasingly important to drug marketers—and thus for drugmakers’ wallets. UCB spent a total of $56.9 million in Bimzelx ads last month, with that split across 53.85% for streaming and 46.15% in linear. 

UCB also took the spot with its immunology therapy in August, although this only counted linear TV promotion, where the company spent $31.2 million at the time. 

Eli Lilly’s recently launched obesity drug Foundayo saw a major jump in September, too, where it has not typically been troubling the top 10, coming in second place. The pharma giant spent $52.5 million on the drug in total, but this was heavily skewed (63.05% of spend) to streaming compared to Lilly's outlay of 36.95% on linear. 

Related

UCB’s Bimzelx comes from out of the blue to claim August’s top pharma ad spending spot

A familiar face in AbbVie’s immunology therapy Skyrizi came in third position, with the company spending $44.7 million altogether. This was, unlike the top two, split in favor of traditional TV ads, with 33.84% spent on streaming and 66.16% linear. 

It was a similar story for AbbVie's second immunology drug Rinvoq, coming in fourth place, with a $40.7 million spending total split 31.91% on streaming and 68.09% on linear.

In fifth and down two spots was Johnson & Johnson’s immunology drug Tremfya, which in the first half of the year had been vying with Skyrizi as the drug with the highest ad spend. 

Spend on Tremfya was only around $400,000 less than Rinvoq for the period, though the majority of this (73.75%) was spent on linear ads. 

Novo’s obesity drug Wegovy jumped back into the top 10 in September in sixth place, while Johnson & Johnson’s atypical antipsychotic drug Caplyta fell two spots to seventh. 

J&J also saw its new oral moderate-to-severe plaque psoriasis drug Icotyde fall two spots down to eighth place with $33.1 million total in spend.

Eli Lilly’s injectable obesity drug Zepbound, not in the top 10 in August, rose up to ninth last month with 81.71% of its total spend of $24.3 million earmarked for linear ads. 

In tenth place, as it was in August, was AbbVie’s neurology drug Vraylar, with $22.3 million spend across streaming and linear.

data.title: Arcutis springs new Zoryve awareness campaign with Simone Biles
data.description:
Arcutis Biotherapeutics has lined up another celeb to tout the benefits of its topical skin medicine Zoryve, adding world-renowned gymnast Simone Biles to its all-star team of spokespeople. 

The company’s “Skin to Believe In” awareness campaign featuring Biles targets the approximately 36 million people in the U.S. who live with inflammatory skin conditions such as seborrheic dermatitis and atopic dermatitis, the most common form of eczema. 

Biles herself spent “years” trying different over-the-counter products to calm her itchy, flaking scalp and dry patches on her arms before getting diagnoses from a dermatologist and finding a steroid-free option that works for her in Zoryve, according to Arcutis. Today, the athlete uses Zoryve in its foam formulation for her seb derm and the cream version for her eczema. 

“I like Zoryve because it is not a steroid, pill, injection, or shampoo and it's easy to use, not greasy, and fits into my routine,” Biles said in a company release. “Using Zoryve reduced the flakes and itching on my scalp, which bothered me the most, and the eczema spots on my arms are also clearer, too.”

Through “Skin to Believe In,” Biles encourages others who may have the inflammatory skin conditions to bring up the topic with a healthcare provider and seek treatment options. 

“I’ve learned that we can’t fix every problem on our own and it’s OK to seek help,” continued Biles. “I believe how you care for yourself reflects how you carry yourself, and by partnering with Arcutis on this awareness campaign I believe we can break the stigma associated with chronic skin conditions by helping people feel empowered to speak with a healthcare provider about their symptoms so that they can find a treatment that works for them.”

According to Arcutis CEO Frank Watanabe, Biles’ first encounter with Zoryve came organically and started on social media. The gymnast opened up about her experience with seborrheic dermatitis and eczema symptoms in a TikTok post around the time of the Paris 2024 Summer Olympics, he explained in an interview. Upon bringing up her itchy, flaky scalp on her large social media platform, dermatologists recognized the seb derm symptoms and encouraged her to check out some of the FDA-approved products available for the condition, which is how she ultimately got started on Zoryve and connected with Arcutis. 

“She’s a very enthusiastic supporter of the product,” Watanabe said. “Working with her is great.” 

Biles isn’t the only Zoryve spokesperson who organically came across the product. So did professional golfer Max Homa and the mother-daughter duo of actress Tori Spelling and her teenage daughter, Stella McDermott. All three are a part of Arcutis’ recent “Free to Be Me” awareness campaign, which looked to bring attention to the skin conditions and help people who may suffer from them recognize the symptoms.  

People with inflammatory skin conditions often don’t realize that they have a treatable medical condition, Watanabe explained, living with symptoms such as itching, sleep disruptions or depression and navigating stigma that can be attached to the visible symptoms of the conditions. Finding a treatment that’s approved for continuous use like Zoryve can be a “real game changer for patients,” the CEO said. 

Related

Arcutis' Zoryve bags 2nd FDA nod, this time as a foam to treat 'the great neglected disease in dermatology'

Amongst its peers in the non-steroid, topical dermatitis crowd, Zoryve is the only product that’s also approved in a foam formulation, which can better reach hard-to-treat areas such as the scalp. So far since its 2023 launch, Zoryve foam already makes up over half of the drug’s total sales, pulling down $67.4 million over the second quarter of 2026 compared to the $62.4 million across Zoryve cream’s various dose strengths. 

“It’s a really unique product,” Watanabe said of Zoryve foam, adding that it “just fits in with patients’ lives.” 

Next year, fast-growing Zoryve could snag another label expansion to cover infants aged three to 24 months with atopic dermatitis, which would be its eighth nod since its initial 2022 approval. This one would cover an area Watanabe knows well; his own son had eczema when he was a baby, meaning he can personally speak to the inconvenience of applying twice-daily topical steroids to young children. Zoryve, meanwhile, has a once-daily application and is already garnering buzz across pediatric dermatologists, who currently “just don’t have good options for these kids,” the CEO said. 

Still, there remains work to be done to grow the addressable patient population as more than half of people with psoriasis, seb derm or eczema aren’t currently seeking treatment, Watanabe noted. To help make treatment options available to people who may not have access to local dermatologists, Arcutis this summer launched a virtual health platform that quickly connects patients with independent dermatologists. 

“We’re helping to make specialized dermatology care a lot more accessible to patients, no matter where that patient is,” Watanabe explained. 

Outside of its awareness campaigns, Zoryve has also been building a name for itself outside of the strictly medical field. This month, Marie Claire magazine bestowed Zoryve cream with its 2026 Best Prescription Skin Solution Award, adding to a stack of similar honors from Allure and Glamour magazine. 

Watanabe attributes Zoryve’s unique recognition in the beauty space to “the thoughtful way that we formulated these products” and notes that the skin market itself is a “very patient-driven sector” that’s subject to a different level of patient engagement due to the visibility of the disease and its response to treatment. Given that, awareness campaigns and recognized spokespeople like Biles can “really help motivate people to seek treatment.”

“When you see someone like Simone, who's so relatable and so I think well-liked and respected, talking about her own condition and what she went through, the struggle she went through, and how going to see a dermatology clinician and getting on prescription treatment has really changed her life for the better. I think it helps people demystify it, destigmatize it,” Watanabe said.

data.title: The Oral GLP-1 Tracker: Prescriptions edge down
data.description:
With the recent launches of Novo Nordisk’s Wegovy pill and Eli Lilly’s Foundayo, the obesity market has started to shift toward oral GLP-1 drugs. While Novo leverages its first-mover advantage with the familiar Wegovy brand, Lilly is betting that the freedom from strict fasting and water requirements can give Foundayo an edge.

Each week, Fierce Pharma’s Oral GLP-1 Tracker will leverage analysts’ notes and IQVIA data to monitor prescription trends and shifting market shares as these two titans vie to become the go-to oral weight-loss solution for millions.

UPDATED: Oct. 9, 2026

Prescriptions for Lilly's Foundayo and Novo's Wegovy pill pulled back a little during last week. 

In its 26th week of launch, Foundayo achieved 57,920 total scripts, down 9.9% sequentially, according to IQVIA data cited by Citi. 

For oral Wegovy, Citi said IQVIA recorded roughly 179K scripts, while Jefferies quoted 180K. To reconcile the discrepancy between the two numbers, we used 179.5K, which translates into a 1.4% weekly decline.

In fact, scripts for all major GLP-1s declined last week across diabetes and obesity care except for Lilly's Zepbound KwikPen, a prefilled injection pen that delivers four fixed weekly doses of tirzepatide, according to Jefferies. Overall Zepbound scrips dipped below 800K in a 0.8% decrease sequentially, just as Novo's total Wegovy scripts fell 2.7% to 505.5K, according to Citi.

Based on the numbers, Jefferies now models $208 million for Foundayo sales in the third quarter, which the team noted is in line with consensus.

UPDATED: Oct. 2, 2026

Eli Lilly's Foundayo is showing clearer signs of acceleration. Total prescriptions for the oral GLP-1 receptor agonist surged about 21% to 64,268 during last week, according to IQVIA data cited by Citi. That haul came off a 13% sequential increase the week before that.

"We're seeing early signs of growth in Q3 for Foundayo," Jefferies analysts wrote in an Oct. 2 note.

Recent expansion of Foundayo could be attributed to a direct-to-consumer ad first aired in late August featuring Martha Stewart, as well as the Medicare GLP-1 Bridge program which, as of July, offers eligible seniors GLP-1 obesity drugs at a $50 monthly copay.

Meanwhile, Novo's Wegovy pill scripts appear stuck at just above $180K. Except for a Labor Day holiday lull, total weekly scripts for the oral semaglutide product have hovered between 181K and 184K over the past five weeks, including 182K last week, according to Citi.

It's worth noting that Foundayo took 25 weeks to reach what the Wegovy pill achieved in just seven weeks in terms of total scripts. But the gap between the two drugs is closing. As Jefferies noted, Lilly owned 26% of the oral obesity market as of last week, versus a little less than 23% in the previous two weeks.

Overall, Lilly's Zepbound remains the obesity market leader with total scripts of 805.7K, up 2.3% sequentially, according to Citi. Novo's total Wegovy scripts for the pill and the injectable were down 0.6% sequentially to a 519.6K.

At the European Association for the Study of Diabetes annual meeting in Milan earlier this week, both Lilly and Novo rolled out multiple data sets touting the blood-sugar, weight-loss, cardiovascular benefits of their GLP-1 programs amid a wave of potential challengers.

UPDATED: Sept. 25, 2026

Total prescriptions for both Eli Lilly's Foundayo and Novo's Wegovy pill have bounced back following a holiday dip and reached new records. Weekly scripts for the Wegov pill jumped 14% sequentially to about 184K, compared with its previous high of 183K, according to IQVIA data cited by Citi. Foundayo climbed 13% to cross 50K for the first time, reaching 53,321.

Foundayo now captures about 1 out of 3 new starts for oral GLP-1 obesity drugs, and “that’s growing week over week,” Lilly CEO David Ricks told CNBC in an interview this week. 

As Leerink Partners analysts noted in a Sept. 23 note, effective Sept. 1, Lilly cut the initial-dose pricing for Foundayo 0.8 mg, 2.5 mg and 5.5 mg to $149, $149 and $199 per month for self-pay patients, respectively. The company framed the promotion as an elasticity experiment and as a push to the first maintenance dose, according to the Leerink note.

As Jefferies analysts pointed out in a Sept. 25 note, the majority of Foundayo scripts seem to be cash pay, with about 80% of patients still on starting doses.

Based on the IQVIA data so far, the Jefferies team estimated U.S. Foundayo revenues of $203 million in the third quarter, slightly lower than the $209 million consensus projection. 

Broadly speaking, Lilly yielded 0.6 percentage point of its obesity market share to Novo during the previous week, but still maintained its share level above 60%, according to Citi. 

In the recently launched Medicare GLP-1 Bridge program, Lilly is capturing 7 out of 10 patients, with many on its Zepbound, Ricks told CNBC. Foundayo, according to Ricks, is attracting Medicare patients looking for convenience but not necessarily a huge weight-loss effect. 

UPDATED: Sept. 18, 2026

As expected, the past U.S. Labor Day holiday took a toll on obesity drugs' prescription numbers. According to IQVIA data cited by Citi, weekly scripts for Novo's Wegovy pill dropped roughly 12% sequentially to about 161K for the last week. The decline for Foundayo was modest, at just 1%, as the Lilly drug still managed to rake in more than 47K scripts. 

Lilly this week said Foundayo captured more than 30% of new patients in the U.S. market for oral obesity ​treatments, Reuters reported. 

Citing Bloomberg Symphony data, Jefferies analysts suggested in a Friday note that Foundayo's recent acceleration "has been driven primarily by retail/commercial channels."

Elsewhere, Lilly's total Zepbound scripts were down 8.5% week over week, but the GIP/GLP-1 drug expanded its market share by 0.4% versus Novo's Wegovy franchise, whose scripts decreased 10% during the period.

UPDATED: Sept. 11, 2026

Both Novo Nordisk’s Wegovy pill and Eli Lilly’s Foundayo saw their highest total prescriptions so far over the past week as the companies’ oral obesity battle continues to play out.  

According to IQVIA data cited by Citi, the Wegovy pill reached an approximate 183K total scripts for the most recent reporting period, versus 181K the week prior. Foundayo, for its part, climbed nearly 8% to reach 47.5K scripts. Citi analysts emphasized that IQVIA may still be missing some Foundayo prescriptions made through telehealth channels. 

Meanwhile, using the last four weeks as a guide, total GLP-1 prescriptions have increased by 5.4%, compared to a 6.8% decline the prior year, the Citi team said. Citi analysts attributed the 12-percentage-point swing to the expansion of oral GLP-1 therapies, which is likely broadening access to the class and drawing in new patients.  

Across the broader landscape, Lilly’s tirzepatide currently holds a nearly 57% share of the total GLP-1 market, compared to around 49.5% last year, while Novo’s semaglutide has stayed relatively flat at a 37% share, the analysts added.  

UPDATED: Sept. 4, 2026

Total prescriptions for Novo Nordisk's Wegovy pill and Eli Lilly's Foundayo both grew over the past week, reaching roughly 181K (+3%) and 44K (+8%), IQVIA data showed, as cited by Citi. Both numbers are the two meds' highest so far. 

While Foundayo has yet to catch up with the Wegovy pill, the market share gap between the two oral drugs is slowly narrowing. According to an Aug. 28 Jefferies note based on data the previous week, Foundayo's share of new prescriptions (NRx), which exclude refills, was 21.5% in the oral obesity market.

Back to the most recent week, the Wegovy pill's position within the Wegovy family remained stable at 35%, as total Wegovy scripts increased 2.7% sequentially to 513.5K. During the same period, Lilly's Zepbound scripts climbed 1.6% to a little fewer than 772K.  

UPDATE: Aug. 28, 2026

Twenty weeks into its launch, Eli Lilly's Foundayo has finally exceeded 40,000 in weekly prescriptions, according to IQVIA data cited by Citi. The oral GLP-1 drug posted 40,862 scripts last week, bouncing back from a small dip the week prior. Still, the drug's scripts level is no match for the roughly 57K that Novo Nordisk's Wegovy pill garnered at week 6 of its own launch.

In its 33rd week of launch, the Wegovy pill booked roughly 175K scripts, slightly down from 176K, per IQVIA. The share of the oral version of semaglutide in all Wegovy obesity scripts was flat week over week at 35%. All told, across the pill and the injectable, Wegovy's weekly scripts were a little over 500K, down 0.8% sequentially.

As Jefferies analysts observed in an Aug. 21 note, Wegovy has been relatively flat since the Medicare GLP-1 Bridge program began July 1.

Overall, the roughly 60%-40% obesity market share split between Lilly and Novo remained stable, as Lilly's Zepbound held its ground as the most popular drug.

UPDATE: Aug. 21, 2026

After a one-week hiccup, Novo Nordisk’s Wegovy pill regained its momentum last week with its largest prescription rate since it was launched in January. There were more than 176,000 prescriptions for the pill in the period, according to data gathered by IQVIA and cited in a note by Citi. 

The oral treatment now accounts for 35% of total Wegovy prescriptions, which is up from 33% the previous week, analysts from Citi said in their weekly update to investors.

Meanwhile, Eli Lilly’s oral GLP-1 Foundayo, which had been on a steady five-week climb, backtracked, with a drop-off from 38,928 prescriptions in the prior period to 36,620 in the latest week.

The movements for the two oral treatments contributed to overall market share adjustments for the companies' diabetes and obesity medicines. While Lilly made a 0.1% gain to 56.7%, Novo increased its market share by 0.3% to 37.1%.  

UPDATE: Aug. 14, 2026

Despite its leading position in the oral GLP-1 market, Novo Nordisk's Wegovy pill seems to be hitting a market share ceiling. For months now, shares of total prescriptions for Wegovy pill within the entire Wegovy franchise have struggled to break through the one-third mark.

While share of oral semaglutide within all Wegovy scripts hit 35% in our previous update, it fell back to 33% last week, as Wegovy pill scripts dropped to about 163K, down from a high of roughly 172K the week prior, according to IQVIA data cited by Citi. 

Total Wegovy scripts, including the original injectable, declined 1.1% sequentially to about 495.5K. As a result, Novo yielded about 0.7 percentage point in obesity market share to Eli Lilly's Zepbound last week based on the IQVIA data. The split stood at 39.9% and 60.1% between Novo and Lilly.

Meanwhile, Lilly's Foundayo continued its upward trajectory with 38,928 total scripts, representing another step up from its previous record of 34,219 set the week prior.

UPDATE: Aug. 7, 2026

Prescriptions for Eli Lilly's Foundayo continue to build, jumping 16% sequentially to 34,219 the previous week, according to IQVIA data cited by Citi. The oral GLP-1 med has been on a roll lately as it appears to celebrate four weeks of consecutive growth in total scripts. However, as Citi noted, there's still a potential gap in IQVIA's capture of telehealth data, and it's not clear how much of the scripts growth was from IQVIA getting better at including those data, or, if the actual growth was much faster in telehealth channels.

This week, Lilly's reported Foundayo sales for the second quarter—$98 million in total, including $67 million in the U.S.—disappointed many. As CEO David Ricks noted on an earnings call, Lilly began broad direct-to-consumer marketing to raise consumer awareness after securing commercial access across the three major pharmacy benefit managers in June. Besides, The Medicare GLP-1 Bridge program went live on July 1, offering coverage for certain weight-loss medications, including Foundayo, for a $50 copayment per month. Ilya Yuffa, president of Lilly USA and global customer capabilities, said the company is "starting to see an inflection point on Foundayo now."

As for Novo Nordisk's Wegovy pill, total scripts recorded by IQVIA have been largely flat with small upticks in the past two weeks, having reached roughly 172K in the previous week. The oral version of semaglutide now makes up 35% of total Wegovy scripts, which take up about 40.6% of the U.S. obesity market share, as Lilly's Zepbound remains the leader. 

UPDATE: July 31, 2026

The small inflection point we noticed two weeks ago regarding Eli Lilly's Foundayo does not appear to be a flash in the pan. Weekly total prescriptions for the small molecule reached 29,388, a new high for the oral GLP-1 receptor agonist after three weeks of consecutive growth, according to IQVIA data cited by Citi. 

As IQVIA may be missing some scripts from telehealth channels, we will get a clearer picture of Foundayo's launch progress when Lilly reports its second-quarter earnings on Wednesday, Aug. 5. Analysts at Jefferies have been modeling $71 million in U.S. sales for the quarter based on IQVIA data.

Meanwhile, Novo Nordisk's Wegovy pill remains far ahead in the oral GLP-1 race with total scripts also hitting a new record of about 171,700, according to Citi. The number represents 1.1% growth from its previous best recorded during the prior week.

Coincidentally, the entire GLP-1 class also saw its total scripts grow 1.1% sequentially across diabetes and obesity uses. Lilly's Zepbound regained some lost ground with total scripts up 1.9% week over week. That's compared to Wegovy, which now makes up 40.6% of the obesity market after a 0.2% sequential decline in total scripts. 

Novo reports earnings on the same day as Lilly, Aug. 5.

UPDATE: July 24, 2026

After a post-holiday lull, prescriptions for GLP-1s have more than bounced back. Weekly prescriptions for Novo Nordisk's Wegovy pill and Eli Lilly's Foundayo reached new highs during the previous week, collecting 169,800 and 26,760, respectively, according to IQVIA data cited by Citi. The two oral drugs' previous records were about 161.5K and 24.3K, respectively. 

Other GLP-1 drugs also enjoyed a boost, as total GLP-1 scripts across obesity and diabetes increased 6.6% sequentially, according to Citi.

From the obesity front, scripts for Lilly's Zepbound rose 7.7% sequentially to about 710K. The GLP-1/GIP dual agonist conceded 0.6 percentage points of market share to Novo but remains ahead of the game with a 58.9% share. That's compared to a 10.5% week-over-week scripts expansion for Novo's Wegovy, which mounted to about 495.5K. In that basket, about 34% belonged to Wegovy pill.

UPDATE: July 17, 2026

Following the Independence Day holiday, the overall GLP-1 market was down 5.1% week over week as measured by total prescriptions across obesity and diabetes uses, according to IQVIA data cited by Citi.

In the obesity field specifically, total scripts for Eli Lilly's Zepbound shrank by 3.1% sequentially to a little below 660K, while Novo Nordisk's Wegovy dipped 4.4% to about 448.5K.

Against this backdrop, Lilly's oral Foundayo seemed to enjoy a small inflection point, with a total 24,303 scripts notably breaking away from its roughly 20K level in the prior five weeks.  

Meanwhile, joining the bigger trend, Wegovy pill scripts dropped to 147.5K during the week, versus about 153K the prior week or 161.5K at its peak. But the contribution of the oral version to the overall Wegovy scripts remained stable at around a third, per Citi's note. 

UPDATE: July 10, 2026

The launch of Eli Lilly’s Foundayo remains “muted,” with weekly prescriptions flat over the last five weeks, analysts from Jefferies said in a July 10 note. The analysis is based on data collected by IQVIA.

In the 13th week of Foundayo’s launch, IQVIA reported 19,550 prescriptions, down for the third straight week after peaking at Week 10 with 21,648 prescriptions. The figure also comes in significantly shy of the Week 13 launch of Novo’s Wegovy pill (more than 105K scripts) and Lilly’s injected obesity treatment Zepbound (59K), but ahead of Novo’s injected Wegovy (13K).

Meanwhile, weekly scripts for Wegovy pill ticked slightly upward sequentially to about 153K, although they still lag behind the drug’s peak of more than 161K.

Jefferies points out that CVS was the last of the big three PBMs to provide coverage of Foundayo, starting on June 1. By contrast, Wegovy had full coverage at the first week of its launch.

While Jefferies’ $71 million quarterly sales projection for Foundayo sits significantly below Wall Street consensus of $130 million, the team still believes that the Lilly med can reach the consensus revenue estimate of $1.2 billion for 2026.

UPDATE: July 6, 2026

For a month now, weekly prescriptions for Eli Lilly's Foundayo have been hovering at around 20,000. In other words, three months into its market debut, the non-peptide GLP-1 receptor agonist was still at the same script level that Novo Nordisk's Wegovy pill had achieved in two to three weeks post-launch.

For the week ended on June 26, Foundayo's total scripts dipped about 4% sequentially to 19,830, according to IQVIA data cited by Jefferies. During the same period, scripts were also down about 2% for oral Wegovy, reaching about 149,000.

In a July 4 report, Jefferies analysts modeled about $71 million in U.S. sales during Foundayo's debut quarter from April to June, versus the team's previous estimate of $85 million in a June 26 report. Wall Street's consensus currently has the number at $130 million. To reach its estimate, Jefferies used an illustrative calculation based on the IQVIA data, with certain assumptions regarding pricing, dosing and stocking.

While Lilly still lags Novo on the oral GLP-1 battlefield, the Indianapolis pharma has maintained a majority 59.5% share of the overall obesity market, according to IQVIA's prescription data.  

As Novo's injectable Wegovy gained about 0.2% scripts (roughly 500) to reach 315,000 for the period, Lilly's Zepbound expanded by 1%, including 375,000 (+3,500) from Zepbound autoinjector and 289,000 (+2,000) from Zepbound DTC Vial+KwikPen.

UPDATE: June 29, 2026

Likely thanks to the Juneteenth federal holiday, prescriptions for both Novo Nordisk's Wegovy pill and Eli Lilly's Foundayo were lower compared with their highest. For the week ended on June 19, Foundayo logged 20,594 total scripts, down from 21,648 the prior week, according to IQVIA data cited by Jefferies. 

For oral Wegovy, the numbers were about 152,000 for the June 19 week, a roughly 9,500 (5.9%) decrease from the prior week. 

As Jefferies' analysts noted, most GLP-1 scripts were down or rather flat in their weekly comparisons. Injectable Wegovy added about 1,000 (0.3%) scripts, landing at 315,000. Mounjaro essentially saw no change, at 804,000.

Lilly has previously noted that it takes time to build awareness for Foundayo as a new brand, whereas Novo benefits from familiarity with the Wegovy moniker. 

Meanwhile, Sandoz just announced that the FDA has accepted its generic tirzepatide autoinjector applications, covering all indications of Lilly's Mounjaro and Zepbound. We'll see how the availability of a generic injectable version shakes up the oral market. 

UPDATE: June 18, 2026

Name recognition and "familiarity" with Novo Nordisk's oral Wegovy has contributed to its rapid uptake in its battle with Lilly's oral GLP-1 Foundayo, according to Spherix analyst Jim Hickey, who conducts monthly surveys with doctors who prescribe the treatments. See Fierce's story on Hickey's analysis here.

UPDATE: June 12, 2026

The share of Novo Nordisk's Wegovy pill among total Wegovy scripts appears to have reached a plateau, hovering around one-third over the past few weeks. The latest number for the week ended on June 5 was 33%, compared with 30%, 32% and 31% in the prior weeks, according to Citi. 

Meanwhile, the obesity market share split between Wegovy and Eli Lilly's Zepbound has been relatively stable at around 40% to 42%, as the Indianapolis pharma's oral Foundayo makes up only a small portion of the market even though its own scripts continue to build. 

Wegovy's total scripts were up 9.8% on a weekly basis, reaching nearly 484,500. Within this haul, Wegovy pill contributed roughly 159,000, the oral version's highest since its launch. The drug's previous highest was 146,000 before dipping to 134,000 in our last update.

Zepbound's scripts also grew week over week by 9.3%, nearing 667,400 for the week. During the same period, IQVIA tracked slightly shy of 20,000 scripts from Foundayo in its ninth week on the market, compared with nearly 17,000 the prior week. 

Thanks to the expansion of the oral version, Wegovy overall now commands 42.1% of the obesity market. Tracing backwards, its share has been climbing steadily, clocking in at 41.9%, 41.2%, 41.4%, 40.5%, 40.4%, 42.6% and 40.4% in the past few weeks.

UPDATE: June 8, 2026

It took just over five months for Novo Nordisk’s Wegovy pill to log 3 million total U.S. prescriptions, underscoring “one of the strongest US pharmaceutical launches by volume on record,” the company announced in a June 7 press release. Meanwhile, Eli Lilly’s rival Foundayo has still yet to achieve more than 17,000 prescriptions, according to a June 5 note from Citi analysts.  

Using data from IQVIA, the analysts tracked 16,982 Foundayo prescriptions as of the drug's eighth week on the market since its April launch. However, the Citi team emphasizes that “there may be a gap in telehealth capture,” as Lilly has previously confirmed to the analysts around 20,000 Foundayo scripts since its launch. Foundayo has been floating around this range for several weeks now since hitting 16,698 at week six, the data show.

Meanwhile, Novo’s Wegovy pill was at 73,544 prescriptions by the time it had hit the same eight-week marker in its own launch. The drug had picked up one million prescriptions 12 weeks after launching and nabbed an additional two million prescriptions in the following ten weeks, Novo said in its release. At its three million total, one prescription is filled roughly every five seconds, the company pointed out in its release. 

Either way, IQVIA’s data suggests a preference for oral formulations in the wider GLP-1 market, with oral Wegovy prescriptions now contributing 30% of total Wegovy scripts, according to the Citi analysts. The oral offering may be driving a wider market for the obesity treatments as well, with Novo explaining in its recent release that more than 80% of its new prescriptions for the Wegovy pill come from people new to GLP-1 therapy. 

June 2 findings from Spherix Global Insights second the notion that oral GLP-1 pills are expanding the overall treatment pool and drawing in a “massive wave of new patients,” the company said in an emailed release. In oral Wegovy’s first four weeks on the market earlier this year, 73% of surveyed primary care physician reported prescribing the med, with over 98% who haven’t yet prescribed it planning to within the next six months, Spherix found. 

“Novo Nordisk’s early performance has set an exceptionally high bar for the competition,” Spherix’s gastroenterology franchise head, Jim Hickey, commented.

On a weekly basis, however, total GLP-1 prescriptions were trending downward over the week of June 1, falling 5.7% week-over-week, Citi analysts noted. Other than the continued rollout of Lilly and Novo’s respective weight loss pills, the analysts cited the effect of the Trump administration’s “most favored nation” pricing policies as a key future event that they think could impact total prescriptions. 

UPDATE: June 1, 2026

In its seventh week on the market, which ended May 22, Eli Lilly’s obesity pill Foundayo continued to track below the pace of Novo Nordisk’s rival Wegovy pill at the same point in its launch.

At the same time, analysts at Jefferies and Citi again flagged caveats that could be skewing the numbers, with the Jefferies team espousing confidence that Lilly’s oral GLP-1 can still meet consensus sales projections for both the second quarter and 2026 as a whole. 

Breaking down the numbers, the Jefferies team put seventh-week total Foundayo prescriptions lower versus the previous week at roughly 11,700, with the clarification that the data’s source, IQVIA, had to use a “best-estimate” tally for the latest week’s prescription trends. 

That trend remains “numerically lower” than the course charted by Novo’s Wegovy pill, which racked up an impressive 67,000 prescriptions in its seventh week, although Foundayo’s performance still tracks ahead of Novo’s injectable Wegovy and Lilly’s first obesity incretin med Zepbound at the same point in their respective rollouts, the analyst team said. 

Lilly has suggested it expects the market for oral obesity meds to “develop over time” and has also cited the time needed to build new brand awareness for Foundayo, according to Jefferies, which added that the Lilly pill’s commercial reimbursement “appears to be ramping more slowly” compared to oral Wegovy. Lilly has confirmed that coverage of Foundayo through CVS Caremark, the United States’ biggest PBM, will begin this week. 

Despite those apparent growing pains, the analysts at Jefferies called Foundayo’s ability to meet consensus sales estimates in the near-term and for the full year as “doable.” The analysts currently predict that Lilly’s oral weight loss med will garner $145 million in the second quarter on the way to a $1.6 billion haul for the full year. 

Consensus estimates are tracking for Q2 and full-year Foundayo sales of $136 million and $1.2 billion, respectively, according to Jefferies. 

On that note, analysts at Citi, have repeatedly warned that IQVIA’s prescription data may be failing to account for telehealth referrals, citing comments from Lilly executives on the total patients they were tracking as of the company’s Q1 earnings call. For its part, Citi placed the total number of Foundayo scripts for the week ending May 22 at roughly 16,000, based on the IQVIA stats. 

By comparison, Novo’s Wegovy pill clocked some 146,000 total scripts over that same seven-day stretch, per Citi. Citi once more flagged that Novo’s Wegovy pill is making up a growing portion of overall semaglutide obesity prescriptions, which the team said points to “preferences for oral formulations.”

UPDATE: May 22, 2026

With both Novo Nordisk’s and Eli Lilly’s oral GLP-1s establishing their footing in the U.S. obesity market, the companies’ respective Wegovy pill and orforglipron tablet Foundayo are making their mark on prescription trends for a class previously confined primarily to injectables.

Looking at the past four weeks, total U.S. GLP-1 prescriptions were up 3.6%, compared to 1.8% at the same time last year, analysts at Citi wrote in a Friday note to clients, citing script tracking data from IQVIA. The Citi team attributed that momentum to the ability of Novo’s and Lilly’s new oral launches to “broaden and reshape the market” for obesity incretin drugs.

As of the week ended May 15, IQVIA logged nearly 17,000 prescriptions for Lilly’s Foundayo, which debuted on April 9. As in prior weeks, the Citi analysts caveated that IQVIA’s data may be missing key prescribing stats from telehealth channels, flagging Lilly executives’ comments during an earnings call at the end of last month that there were then roughly 20,000 patients on the new oral therapy.

Conversely, Novo’s Wegovy pill has recorded roughly 142,000 prescriptions as of last week, according to Citi’s note.

In an apparent sign of the new oral option's popularity, the analysts flagged that oral Wegovy now comprises 31% of total prescriptions for the brand, which is otherwise administered as an injection. The Citi team noted that this trend could signal “preferences for oral formulations.”

Meanwhile, scoping out the broader U.S. GLP-1 market over the past four weeks, Lilly’s tirzepatide brand—which includes both Zepbound for obesity and Mounjaro for Type 2 diabetes—now holds a 54.8% share compared to a 47% piece of the pie last year. Novo’s U.S. market share for semaglutide has remained “relatively flat” over that stretch and clocked in at 37.4%, per Citi.

Week over week, total GLP-1 prescriptions were down a little less than 1% in the U.S. Looking at obesity specifically, Citi’s analysts flagged a 2.1% tirzepatide prescription decline versus last week, while Novo’s Wegovy prescriptions tracked at a positive 1.8%.

Aside from both companies' oral GLP-1 launches continuing to add texture to the market, the analysts noted that the effect of the Trump administration’s “most favored nation” pricing policies on Novo’s and Lilly’s drugs could boost overall prescriptions for the class. 

UPDATE: May 15, 2026

Total prescriptions for Eli Lilly’s Foundayo reached 10,248 for the week that ended May 8, up from 7,335 the prior week, according to IQVIA data cited by Citi. While still on the rise, Foundayo’s growth pace continued to lag behind that of Novo Nordisk’s Wegovy pill during the same stage of their launch. 

Wegovy’s total scripts rose by 1.3% week over week to nearly 446,000, as its share in the obesity GLP-1 market climbed 0.1 percentage point to 40.5%, according to Citi.

However, Wegovy’s growth apparently didn’t come from its oral formulation. Wegovy pill scripts landed at about 137,000 for the week, down from roughly 143,000 the prior week, marking the first time that the pill's scripts have fallen since the oral launch in early January.

Scripts from the Wegovy pill made up 31% of total Wegovy scripts for the period, down 2 percentage points from the previous week. Still, Citi analysts argued that this roughly one-third of share “suggests preferences for oral formulations.”

Even as Wegovy gained ground, Lilly’s Zepbound remained the obesity market leader, with 59.5% share, as its nearly 656,000 scripts marked 0.8% growth week over week. 

UPDATE: May 8, 2026

As Eli Lilly’s Foundayo finds its footing on the market, Novo Nordisk’s own Wegovy pill—which got a three-month head start to launch over its rival this year—is starting to illuminate just how significant an oral GLP-1 may be to the lucrative obesity drug landscape. 

In the fourth week since its April 9 debut in the U.S., Lilly’s Foundayo has generated 7,335 total prescriptions, analysts at Citi wrote in a note to clients Friday, citing prescribing stats from IQVIA. 

That ramp-up looks slower on paper than that enjoyed by the Wegovy pill during its initial rollout, but the Citi team cautioned that there may be a gap in IQVIA data linked to telehealth prescriptions for Lilly’s tablet. They pointed to comments from Lilly executives late last week indicating that there were now some 20,000 patients on Foundayo, with the company noting that telehealth platforms were generating some 35% of the oral GLP-1 medicine’s current launch volume. 

The analysts acknowledged that Lilly’s early Foundayo prescription trends “continue to build,” while adding that they “look for further growth to develop the oral competitive market.” 

During its earnings call last week, Lilly added that upcoming coverage secured at major pharmacy benefit managers should come online by the middle of May, providing a likely sizeable tailwind to Foundayo’s trajectory. 

As for Novo, the company logged some 440,410 Wegovy prescriptions on the week that ended May 1, with oral Wegovy now making up 33% of those total obesity referrals, per the Citi analysts, who said that trend could reflect “preferences for oral formulations.”

The update on the oral obesity numbers comes after Novo earlier this week reported that the Wegovy pill generated 2.26 billion Danish kroner (around $355 million) in its first quarter on the U.S. market. 

For its part, Foundayo will likely need to start generating around 22,000 prescriptions a week in order to hit current consensus forecasts of $160 million in second-quarter sales, RBC Capital Markets’ Trung ​Huynh said this week, as cited by Reuters. 

UPDATE: May 4, 2026

With three weeks of data on Lilly’s oral GLP-1 launch in obesity now on the books, the dimensions of Foundayo’s rollout—and its critical comparison to that of Novo Nordisk’s Wegovy pill—are coming into focus. 

In its third week on the U.S. market, which ended April 24, Foundayo generated some 5,600 prescriptions, analysts at Jefferies wrote in a May 1 note to clients. That level of adoption is numerically lower than the stats recorded by the Wegovy pill in its third week, when prescriptions for the oral obesity med came in at around 26,100, per the note. 

Nevertheless, almost all of Foundayo’s recorded performance stems from cash pay channels, according to the Jefferies team, with commercial access via insurance set to come online by the middle of this month, which will likely give Foundayo a substantial boost in uptake. 

The team acknowledged that Foundayo’s reimbursement “appears to be ramping more slowly vs oral Wegovy’s.” 

Overall, the analysts described Foundayo as “off to a solid start,” and estimate the drug will generate $146 million in the second quarter and $1.6 billion for all of 2026. That compares to consensus forecasts of $134 million and $1.2 billion, respectively. 

Lilly told the Jefferies team that, as of week three of its launch, some 45% of Foundayo prescriptions were coming through its direct-to-patient channel LillyDirect, alongside 35% of referrals from telehealth providers and the remaining 20% coming from traditional retail venues. 

During an earnings call with analysts last week, Lilly executives noted that there were around 20,000 patients on Foundayo in the U.S. The drug was approved April 1. 

As for Novo’s pill, oral Wegovy lassoed around 135,000 total prescriptions during the week that ended April 24, according to the Jefferies notes. 

UPDATE: April 24, 2026

Eli Lilly’s oral GLP-1 obesity treatment Foundayo has attracted 3,707 prescriptions though its second week on the market, lagging far behind the pace of Novo Nordisk’s GLP-1 pill Wegovy, which drew 18,410 prescriptions though its second week on the market in January. 

The results were made available by Jefferies from healthcare analytics firm IQVIA and are good through the week ending on April 17.

With the result, Lilly’s shares dipped by 4% on Friday, compared to a 7% gain for Novo.

Foundayo’s launch so far does compare favorably to that of Novo’s injected Wegovy, which numbered 1,578 prescriptions through two weeks when it reached the market in the U.S. but falls short of Lilly’s Zepbound pen, which counted 7,292 prescriptions through its second week.

In its note to investors, analysts from Jefferies called the result “disappointing vs. expectations."

Brand recognition has played a role, according to Bernstein analyst Courtney Breen, who said that online searches for GLP-1 drugs peaked during Wegovy’s launch, potentially boosting demand.

UPDATE: April 21, 2026

Eli Lilly’s oral GLP-1 Foundayo is off to a solid launch, drawing 1,390 prescriptions in its first week on the market, according to tracking figures from IQVIA and presented by Jefferies. The tabulation is from the week starting April 6. This compares to the 3,071 prescriptions Novo Nordisk garnered during its Wegovy pill launch week in January.

While Foundayo came up short in this oral GLP-1 launch week comparison, it did exceed the number of prescriptions recorded in the first week of the launch of both Lilly’s injected Zepbound (1,100) and Novo’s injected version of Wegovy (768).

In a note to clients, analysts with Jefferies cautioned that comparisons can be “tricky” given that oral Wegovy was launched at the start of the year and that initial capture rates from IQVIA are “volatile” and may not include product sampling. 

“Overall, we think Foundayo’s initial scripts look excellent,” the Jefferies team wrote, adding that it is modeling Foundayo’s sales to reach $1.6 billion this year, compared to a consensus of $1.5 billion, with its peak annual sales topping out at $30 billion versus the consensus of $26 billion. 

“We think the real opportunity for Foundayo is ex-U.S., given its clear advantages on scale, distribution and [cost of goods sold],” Jefferies wrote.
